In this sample code document, I generate the accurate isochrone mapping.

1 Network

I use the real network data I will work on later. The resolution is max 10 meter (i.e., some segments are shorter than 10 meters).

The data source here is swiss tlm3d, which is most precise among potential data sets https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/en/landscape-model-swisstlm3d. Data in this document has been clipped by the boundary of Canton ZH.

I refer to Objektkatalog swissTLM3D 2.2 (in German). Attributes here are translated based on my kindergarten-level German by DeepL. I also refer to descriptions in Road Map 1:200’000 (Federal Office of Topography swisstopo), because there is an English version.

The road segments are generally classified in streets (strassen in German) and ways (wege in German). The usable classification is road width (from 1 to 10).

I refer to the paper https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ufug.2018.07.007. In the section Weighted-path strategy, Appendix A. ODD model documentation, they mentioned they organized an expert panel to value pedestrian mobility for different road types.

The scale ranged from 1 indicating a strong preference by the respective users to 5 indicating a strong avoidance.

Although some road type (e.g., 10m street and Cantonal road) get a high grade, but the authors didn’t claim these roads are not walkable. In that case, I temporarily consider all roads are walkable.

A minor supplement: if I considered car accessibility later, the threshold for road width would be 4 meter. Now I will leave it here.

2 Baseline: Isochrones under a constant speed

In my research proposal, I refer to the paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/nature25181. The principle is:

The land-cover-dependent travel speeds were then adjusted to take into account the effect of topographical properties.

But in most paper, tobler walking function can be calculated via raster data instead of network data.

Then I get the idea from the paper: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0284630 (see details in the section 4.4. Network costs imputation and 4.5. Network topology construction).

In MSc Sample Code: Reachable Area, I have generated the isochrone map based on a constant speed and time limit.

I will use the shortest paths within that reachable area as my baseline.

The maximum walking speed is 6 * exp(-3.5 * abs(-0.05 + 0.05)) = 6 km/h (1.666667 m/s) in Tobler’s formulation. This value is also close to the fast pace of older adults with obstacles https://agsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1532-5415.2005.53157.x (i.e., 1.16 ± 0.34 m/s) and https://www.bmj.com/content/339/bmj.b4460.short (i.e., >= 1.85m/s for men and >= 1.5m/s for women).

So I set 1.7 m/s as the baseline speed.

I first run the baseline result.

Then I write a function to convert that list to an sf object.

Code 
# Function to convert a list of isochrones into an sf object
convert_iso_list_to_sf <- function(iso_list, points_sf, speed_mps, time_limits) {
  
  # Flatten list and add attributes
  iso_sf <- purrr::map2_dfr(seq_along(iso_list), iso_list, function(i, isochrones) {
    if (is.null(isochrones)) return(NULL)  # Skip empty results
    
    # Get the home ID from points_sf
    p_id <- points_sf$id[i]
    
    # Convert nested list into sf
    purrr::map2_dfr(time_limits, isochrones, function(time, iso_poly) {
      if (is.null(iso_poly) || nrow(iso_poly) == 0) return(NULL)  # Skip empty polygons
      
      # Add attributes
      iso_poly <- iso_poly %>%
        dplyr::mutate(
          id = p_id,
          speed_mps = speed_mps,
          time_limit_s = time,
        )
      
      return(iso_poly)
    })
  })
  
  return(iso_sf)
}

Get sf object as baseline result.

Then I map it for each home location.

# Generate separate maps for each unique ID
maps <- purrr::map(unique_ids, function(uid) {
  home_map <- mapview::mapview(homes[homes$id == uid, ], col.regions = "black", layer.name = paste0("Home_", uid))
  iso_map <- mapview::mapview(iso_sf[iso_sf$id == uid, ], color = "black", col.regions = "white", lwd = 3, layer.name = paste0("Iso_15min_", uid)) # 15 here means 15 mins
  
  home_map + iso_map  # Combine both layers for this ID
})

3 Isochrone with elevation factor

Since the elevation factor is also nondirect, the approach is similar as before. We only need to consider elevation factor into speed calculation (edge-based).

Code 
# Function to compute isochrones efficiently considering elevation factor
# set 900 seconds as time limit
compute_isochrones_ele <- function(speed_mps, points_sf, net, time_limits = c(900)) {
  
  # Function to compute isochrones for a single home location
  compute_iso_for_point <- function(p) {
    
    # Define max possible travel distance for the longest time limit
    max_travel_dist <- (base::ceiling(max(time_limits) * speed_mps / 50) * 50 )# Round to nearest 50m
    
    # Create a buffer around the home point
    buffer_zone <- sf::st_buffer(p, max_travel_dist)
    
    # Convert clipped, segmented road network to sfnetwork
    filtered <- net %>% sfnetworks::activate("edges") %>% 
      sf::st_filter(buffer_zone, .pred = st_intersects) %>%
      sfnetworks::activate("nodes") %>%
      dplyr::filter(!tidygraph::node_is_isolated()) 
    
    # add constant speed and time column
    # use `elevation_adjustment_factor` to adjust speed
    filtered <- filtered |> sfnetworks::activate("edges") |>
      dplyr::mutate(speed = units::set_units(speed_mps, "m/s")) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(time = weight / (speed * elevation_adjustment_factor)) %>%
      sfnetworks::activate("nodes")  # Activate nodes for distance calculations
    
    # Find nearest node in the local network
    home_node <- sf::st_nearest_feature(p, filtered)
    
    # Compute isochrones using purrr::map()
    isochrones <- purrr::map(time_limits, ~ {
      filtered %>%
        sfnetworks::activate("nodes") %>%
        dplyr::filter(tidygraph::node_distance_from(home_node, weights = time) <= .x) %>%
        sf::st_geometry() %>%
        sf::st_combine() %>%
        sf::st_concave_hull(0.3) %>%
        sf::st_as_sf()
    })
      
      return(isochrones)
    }
    iso_results <- purrr::map(seq_len(nrow(points_sf)), ~ compute_iso_for_point(points_sf[.x, ]))
+   
+   return(iso_results) # a list of polygons for each point in points_sf
  }

Now I compute isochrone with elevation factor.

I then convert list to sf objects (same as before).

Now I compare baseline isochrone and elevation isochrone together. The reachable area reduces a bit, but there is only a minor difference in mapping (since leaflet is based on wgs84).

Code 
# Generate separate maps for each unique ID
# I name the map as 01, because I add another one layer from baseline layer (home point + baseline isochrone)

maps_01 <- purrr::map(unique_ids, function(uid) {
  home_map <- mapview::mapview(homes[homes$id == uid, ], col.regions = "black", layer.name = paste0("Home_", uid)) # home location
  
  iso_map_base <- mapview::mapview(iso_sf[iso_sf$id == uid, ], color = "black", col.regions = "white", lwd = 2, layer.name = paste0("Base_15min_", uid)) # 15 here means 15 mins
  
  iso_map_ele <- mapview::mapview(iso_sf_ele[iso_sf_ele$id == uid, ], color = "lightblue", col.regions = "lightgreen", layer.name = paste0("Elev_15min_", uid)) # 15 here means 15 mins
  
  home_map + iso_map_base + iso_map_ele # Combine both layers for this ID
})

# latticeView will render small multiples without synchronising
leafsync::latticeView(maps_01)

Since the operation later are based on paths, I will use my filtered network. Also, please skip the map below if you had trypophobia. The network is precise with density nodes.

4 Before Tobler Hiking Function: Path Generation

Now I have generated all shortest paths from home to nodes in the baseline reachable area.

Now I have generated candidate paths.Data structure and example mapping will be shown later after calculation.

Based on paths, I start accessibility estimation under Tobler Hiking Function.

5 Tobler hiking function

See more about Tobler hiking function: https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?repid=rep1&type=pdf&doi=15a01b57bba9c8e19e160e3281071b73e36a4387.

The slope is measured as rise/run, i.e., dh/dx or tan(theta). Thus, the slope can vary by directions (e.g., uphill from node 1 to node 2, then downhill from node 2 to node 1, for the same road segment (edge)).

My initial attempt is adding both uphill and downhill speed and travel time in edge attributes (as data I have shown before). Then I find I should determine directions first. With certain paths, I can determine directions or calculate slope accurately based on nodes.

Thus, I use isochrone under a constant speed as baseline. I exclude some “definitely reachable” nodes (under lowest tobler function and elevation factor) and generate all shortest paths within that area.

For each path, I can calculate travel time step by step under slice it with a certain threshold.

How it works?

Even though I am working on the filtered network, there are 20898 paths as coarse paths.

So I use vctrs and purrr for quicker operations.

Come back to the data structure. paths_speeds_and_times_all is a list with 20898 elements.

For each path (format as paths_speeds_and_times_all[[X]], X is the number of path), it has lists inside (format as paths_speeds_and_times_all[[X]][[“attribute”]], X is the number of path).

“Attributes” here contain all attributes I calculate before (slope, distance, mean_elev, elev_factor, speed, travel_time).

Now I will show a basic example: how slope varies among different steps.

I still use that candidate path as the example. The total travel time from green to orange under tobler hiking function is:

Code 
sum(paths_speeds_and_times_all[[1]][["travel_time"]])
[1] 1623.895

It obviously exceeds our max threshold 15 min (900 second). So now I will slice paths based on three thresholds, 300 (5 min), 600 (10 min), and 900 (15 min).

Code 
slice_path_by_time <- function(path, time_limit) {
  # Compute cumulative travel time along the path
  accumulated_time <- cumsum(path$travel_time)
  
  # Find the first index where accumulated time exceeds time_limit
  slice_index <- which(accumulated_time > time_limit)[1] - 1
  
  # If no time limit is exceeded, take the full path
  if (is.na(slice_index) || slice_index <= 0) {
    return(NULL)  # Return NULL to indicate no valid path
  }
  
  # Slice indices safely
  indices <- seq_len(slice_index)

  # Return the sliced path with node_paths & edge_paths included
  return(list(
    node_paths = path$node_paths[indices],
    edge_paths = path$edge_paths[indices],
    speed = path$speed[indices],
    travel_time = path$travel_time[indices],
    total_time = accumulated_time[indices]
  ))
}

# Apply function to all paths while filtering out NULL results
apply_slice_to_all_paths <- function(paths_data, time_limits) {
  result <- map(time_limits, function(time_limit) {
    sliced_paths <- map(paths_data, ~ slice_path_by_time(.x, time_limit)) %>%
      compact()  # Remove NULL results
    return(sliced_paths)
  })
  
  # Assign names for each time limit
  names(result) <- paste0("time_limit_", time_limits, "sec")
  
  return(result)
}

Then how it works? sliced_paths_by_time is still list, with three lists named by time limit. Each list here (e.g., sliced_paths_by_time[[“time_limit_300sec”]][[1]]) stores sliced paths under a certain time limit based on cumsum time. So, 300-second one is the longest (20530), then 600-second one (18372), and the 900-second ha least paths (14156).

Code 
# 1. Function to create an isochrone polygon for the given path nodes (concave hull)
create_isochrone <- function(nodes, alpha = 0.3) {
  # Convert nodes to geometry and create a concave hull
  iso_polygon <- nodes %>%
    sf::st_geometry() %>%
    sf::st_combine() %>%
    sf::st_concave_hull(alpha) %>%
    st_as_sf()
  return(iso_polygon)
}

# 2. Create isochrones for each time limit
create_isochrones_for_all_paths <- function(sliced_paths_by_time, nodes_sf, node_df) {
  isochrones_list <- list()  # Initialize an empty list to store the isochrones
  
  for (time_limit in names(sliced_paths_by_time)) {
    sliced_paths <- sliced_paths_by_time[[time_limit]]
    
    # Step 1: Extract all node indices from all paths
    all_node_indices <- sliced_paths %>%
      map(~ .x$node_paths) %>%  # Extract node_paths from all paths
      unlist() %>%  # Flatten list
      unique()  # Keep only unique node IDs
    
    # Step 2: Retrieve corresponding coordinates from node_df
    unique_nodes_df <- node_df %>%
      filter(node_id %in% all_node_indices) %>%
      select(x, y)  # Keep only coordinates
    
    # Step 3: Convert unique nodes to an sf object
    unique_nodes_sf <- st_as_sf(unique_nodes_df, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = st_crs(nodes_sf))
    
    # Step 4: Generate the isochrone polygon from the unique nodes
    isochrone <- create_isochrone(unique_nodes_sf)
    
    # Store the isochrone in the list
    isochrones_list[[time_limit]] <- isochrone
  }
  
  return(isochrones_list)
}

6 Tobler hiking function with elevation factor

Similar with the last session, but I multiply speed with elevation factor.

Code 
# 3️⃣ Fully vectorized function to compute speed & travel timeincluding elevation facto
calculate_path_speeds_and_times_elev <- function(path) {
  path_df <- calculate_slopes_distances(path) %>%
    mutate(
      slope = slope,
      mean_elev = mean_elev,
      elev_factor = elev_factor,
      speed = elev_factor * tobler_hiking_function(slope),  # Tobler function
      travel_time = distance / speed  # Travel time
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      node_paths = path[-length(path)],  # Store node paths
      edge_paths = path[-1]  # Store edge paths
    )

  return(path_df)
}

# Baseline: Isochrones under a constant speed

In my research proposal, I refer to the paper: <https://doi.org/10.1038/nature25181>. The principle is:

> The land-cover-dependent travel speeds were then adjusted to take into account the effect of topographical properties.

But in most paper, tobler walking function can be calculated via raster data instead of network data.

Then I get the idea from the paper: <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0284630> (see details in the section 4.4. Network costs imputation and 4.5. Network topology construction).

In `MSc Sample Code: Reachable Area`, I have generated the isochrone map based on a constant speed and time limit.

I will use the shortest paths within that reachable area as my baseline.

The maximum walking speed is 6 * exp(-3.5 * abs(-0.05 + 0.05)) = 6 km/h (1.666667 m/s) in Tobler’s formulation. This value is also close to the fast pace of older adults with obstacles <https://agsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1532-5415.2005.53157.x> (i.e., 1.16 ± 0.34 m/s) and <https://www.bmj.com/content/339/bmj.b4460.short> (i.e., >= 1.85m/s for men and >= 1.5m/s for women).

So I set 1.7 m/s as the baseline speed.

```{r function compute isochrones, include=FALSE}
# Function to compute isochrones efficiently
# set 900 seconds as time limit (15 min)
compute_isochrones <- function(speed_mps, points_sf, net, time_limits = c(900)) {
  
  # Function to compute isochrones for a single home location
  compute_iso_for_point <- function(p, point_id) {
    
    # Define max possible travel distance for the longest time limit
    max_travel_dist <- (base::ceiling(max(time_limits) * speed_mps / 50) * 50 )# Round to nearest 50m
    
    # Create a buffer around the home point
    buffer_zone <- sf::st_buffer(p, max_travel_dist)
    
    # Convert clipped, segmented road network to sfnetwork
    filtered <- net |> sfnetworks::activate("edges") |> 
      sf::st_filter(buffer_zone, .pred = st_intersects) |>
      sfnetworks::activate("nodes") |>
      dplyr::filter(!tidygraph::node_is_isolated()) 
    
    # Save filtered network as RDS file in the current directory
    file_name <- paste0("id", point_id, "_filtered_net.rds")  # Construct file name
    saveRDS(filtered, file_name)  # Save to file
    
    # Add constant speed and time column
    filtered <- filtered |> sfnetworks::activate("edges") |>
      dplyr::mutate(speed = units::set_units(speed_mps, "m/s")) |>
      dplyr::mutate(time = weight / speed) %>%
      sfnetworks::activate("nodes")  # Activate nodes for distance calculations
    
    # Find nearest node in the local network
    home_node <- sf::st_nearest_feature(p, filtered)
    
    # Compute isochrones using purrr::map()
    isochrones <- purrr::map(time_limits, ~ {
      filtered |>
        sfnetworks::activate("nodes") |>
        dplyr::filter(tidygraph::node_distance_from(home_node, weights = time) <= .x) |>
        sf::st_geometry() |>
        sf::st_combine() |>
        sf::st_concave_hull(0.3) |>
        sf::st_as_sf()
    })
    
    return(isochrones)
  }
  
  # Apply function to all points in points_sf
  iso_results <- purrr::map2(seq_len(nrow(points_sf)), points_sf$id, ~ compute_iso_for_point(points_sf[.x, ], .y))
  
  return(iso_results) # a list of polygons for each point in points_sf
}
```

I first run the baseline result.

```{r baseline result, include=FALSE}
iso_results <- compute_isochrones(1.7, p, net)
```

Then I write a function to convert that list to an `sf` object.

```{r function baseline list to sf}
# Function to convert a list of isochrones into an sf object
convert_iso_list_to_sf <- function(iso_list, points_sf, speed_mps, time_limits) {
  
  # Flatten list and add attributes
  iso_sf <- purrr::map2_dfr(seq_along(iso_list), iso_list, function(i, isochrones) {
    if (is.null(isochrones)) return(NULL)  # Skip empty results
    
    # Get the home ID from points_sf
    p_id <- points_sf$id[i]
    
    # Convert nested list into sf
    purrr::map2_dfr(time_limits, isochrones, function(time, iso_poly) {
      if (is.null(iso_poly) || nrow(iso_poly) == 0) return(NULL)  # Skip empty polygons
      
      # Add attributes
      iso_poly <- iso_poly %>%
        dplyr::mutate(
          id = p_id,
          speed_mps = speed_mps,
          time_limit_s = time,
        )
      
      return(iso_poly)
    })
  })
  
  return(iso_sf)
}
```

Get `sf` object as baseline result.

```{r baseline result sf, include=FALSE}
# Compute isochrones as sf polygons

iso_sf <- iso_sf |> dplyr::mutate(area = sf::st_area(x)) |> dplyr::rename(geometry = x) |> dplyr::mutate(elevation = FALSE)
iso_sf
```

```{r baseline result mapping}
unique_ids <- base::intersect(p$id, iso_sf$id)  # Common IDs

# Generate separate maps for each unique ID
maps <- purrr::map(unique_ids, function(uid) {
  home_map <- mapview::mapview(homes[homes$id == uid, ], col.regions = "black", layer.name = paste0("Home_", uid))
  iso_map <- mapview::mapview(iso_sf[iso_sf$id == uid, ], color = "black", col.regions = "white", lwd = 3, layer.name = paste0("Iso_15min_", uid)) # 15 here means 15 mins
  
  home_map + iso_map  # Combine both layers for this ID
})

# latticeView will render small multiples without synchronising
# feel free to move each facet!
leafsync::latticeView(maps)
```
# Isochrone with elevation factor

Since the elevation factor is also nondirect, the approach is similar as before. We only need to consider elevation factor into speed calculation (edge-based).

```{r function isochrone with elev}
# Function to compute isochrones efficiently considering elevation factor
# set 900 seconds as time limit
compute_isochrones_ele <- function(speed_mps, points_sf, net, time_limits = c(900)) {
  
  # Function to compute isochrones for a single home location
  compute_iso_for_point <- function(p) {
    
    # Define max possible travel distance for the longest time limit
    max_travel_dist <- (base::ceiling(max(time_limits) * speed_mps / 50) * 50 )# Round to nearest 50m
    
    # Create a buffer around the home point
    buffer_zone <- sf::st_buffer(p, max_travel_dist)
    
    # Convert clipped, segmented road network to sfnetwork
    filtered <- net %>% sfnetworks::activate("edges") %>% 
      sf::st_filter(buffer_zone, .pred = st_intersects) %>%
      sfnetworks::activate("nodes") %>%
      dplyr::filter(!tidygraph::node_is_isolated()) 
    
    # add constant speed and time column
    # use `elevation_adjustment_factor` to adjust speed
    filtered <- filtered |> sfnetworks::activate("edges") |>
      dplyr::mutate(speed = units::set_units(speed_mps, "m/s")) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(time = weight / (speed * elevation_adjustment_factor)) %>%
      sfnetworks::activate("nodes")  # Activate nodes for distance calculations
    
    # Find nearest node in the local network
    home_node <- sf::st_nearest_feature(p, filtered)
    
    # Compute isochrones using purrr::map()
    isochrones <- purrr::map(time_limits, ~ {
      filtered %>%
        sfnetworks::activate("nodes") %>%
        dplyr::filter(tidygraph::node_distance_from(home_node, weights = time) <= .x) %>%
        sf::st_geometry() %>%
        sf::st_combine() %>%
        sf::st_concave_hull(0.3) %>%
        sf::st_as_sf()
    })
      
      return(isochrones)
    }
    iso_results <- purrr::map(seq_len(nrow(points_sf)), ~ compute_iso_for_point(points_sf[.x, ]))
+   
+   return(iso_results) # a list of polygons for each point in points_sf
  }
```

Now I compute isochrone with elevation factor.

```{r list iso with elev, include=FALSE}

```

```{r sf iso with elev, include=FALSE}
iso_sf_ele
```

# Before Tobler Hiking Function: Path Generation

Now I have generated all shortest paths from home to nodes in the baseline reachable area.


Now I have generated candidate paths.Data structure and example mapping will be shown later after calculation.

Based on paths, I start accessibility estimation under Tobler Hiking Function.

# Tobler hiking function

See more about Tobler hiking function: <https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?repid=rep1&type=pdf&doi=15a01b57bba9c8e19e160e3281071b73e36a4387>.

The slope is measured as rise/run, i.e., dh/dx or tan(theta). Thus, the slope can vary by directions (e.g., uphill from node 1 to node 2, then downhill from node 2 to node 1, for the same road segment (edge)).

My initial attempt is adding both uphill and downhill speed and travel time in edge attributes (as data I have shown before). Then I find I should determine directions first. With certain paths, I can determine directions or calculate slope accurately based on nodes.

Thus, I use isochrone under a constant speed as baseline. I exclude some "definitely reachable" nodes (under lowest tobler function and elevation factor) and generate all shortest paths within that area. 

For each path, I can calculate travel time step by step under slice it with a certain threshold.

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Extract node coordinates and elevations as a dataframe
nodes_df <- net %>%
  sfnetworks::activate("nodes") %>%
  sf::st_as_sf() %>%  # Convert to sf object
  dplyr::mutate(
    x = sf::st_coordinates(.)[, 1],  # Extract X
    y = sf::st_coordinates(.)[, 2]   # Extract Y
  ) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%  # Convert back to tibble
  tibble::rownames_to_column("node_id") %>%  # Assign unique node ID safely
  dplyr::mutate(node_id = as.integer(node_id)) %>%  # Ensure numeric ID
  sf::st_drop_geometry()  # Keep only necessary columns

# Convert to named vectors for fast lookup (eliminates joins)
node_elevation <- setNames(nodes_df$elevation, nodes_df$node_id)
node_x <- setNames(nodes_df$x, nodes_df$node_id)
node_y <- setNames(nodes_df$y, nodes_df$node_id)

# 2️⃣ Faster slope & distance calculation using named vectors
calculate_slopes_distances <- function(path) {
  node1 <- path[-length(path)]
  node2 <- path[-1]

  # Direct lookup (much faster than joins)
  elevation1 <- vctrs::vec_slice(node_elevation, node1)
  elevation2 <- vctrs::vec_slice(node_elevation, node2)
  mean_elev <- (elevation1 + elevation2)/2
  elev_factor <- 1.016 * exp(-0.0001072 * mean_elev)
  x1 <- vctrs::vec_slice(node_x, node1)
  y1 <- vctrs::vec_slice(node_y, node1)
  x2 <- vctrs::vec_slice(node_x, node2)
  y2 <- vctrs::vec_slice(node_y, node2)

  # Vectorized distance & slope calculation
  distance <- sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)
  slope <- (elevation2 - elevation1) / distance

  return(tibble(node1, node2, slope, distance, mean_elev, elev_factor))
}

# 3️⃣
tobler_hiking_function <- function(slope) {
  # Tobler's hiking function: speed in km/h
  speed_kmh <- 6 * exp(-3.5 * abs(slope + 0.05))
  # Convert to m/s
  speed_ms <- speed_kmh * 1000 / 3600
  return(speed_ms)
}

# 3️⃣ Fully vectorized function to compute speed & travel time
calculate_path_speeds_and_times <- function(path) {
  path_df <- calculate_slopes_distances(path) %>%
    mutate(
      slope = slope,
      mean_elev = mean_elev,
      elev_factor = elev_factor,
      speed = tobler_hiking_function(slope),  # Tobler function
      travel_time = distance / speed  # Travel time
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      node_paths = path[-length(path)],  # Store node paths
      edge_paths = path[-1]  # Store edge paths
    )

  return(path_df)
}
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# 4️⃣ Apply to all paths in parallel, ensuring node_paths and edge_paths are stored
paths_speeds_and_times_all <- paths %>%
  dplyr::pull(node_paths) %>%
  purrr::map(~ calculate_path_speeds_and_times(.x))
```

How it works?

Even though I am working on the filtered network, there are 20898 paths as coarse paths. 

So I use `vctrs` and `purrr` for quicker operations.

Come back to the data structure. `paths_speeds_and_times_all` is a list with 20898 elements. 

For each path (format as paths_speeds_and_times_all[[X]], X is the number of path), it has lists inside (format as paths_speeds_and_times_all[[X]][["attribute"]], X is the number of path). 

"Attributes" here contain all attributes I calculate before (slope, distance, mean_elev, elev_factor, speed, travel_time).

Now I will show a basic example: how slope varies among different steps.

```{r mapping slope, include=FALSE}
# take one path as example
# 1. Access the edges involved in the first path and convert to sf
first_path_edges <- edges_sf %>%
  dplyr::slice(paths$edge_paths[[1]]) %>%
  sf::st_as_sf()  # Convert edges to sf

# 2. Associate each edge with its corresponding speed from paths_speeds[[1]]
edges_with_speeds <- first_path_edges %>%
  mutate(slope = paths_speeds_and_times_all[[1]][["slope"]])  # Add the speeds to the edges

# 3. Create a custom color column based on the speed
edges_with_speeds <- edges_with_speeds %>%
  mutate(slope_color = case_when(
    slope > 0.1 ~ "uphill",   # only show obvious uphill
    slope < 0 ~ "downhill",  # then downhill
    TRUE ~ "flat"          # others as flat
  ))

# 4. Extract the coordinates of the first and last nodes in the path
start_node_coords <- st_coordinates(net %>% activate("nodes") %>% slice(paths$node_paths[[1]][1]))
end_node_coords <- st_coordinates(net %>% activate("nodes") %>% slice(paths$node_paths[[1]][length(paths$node_paths[[1]])]))

# 5. Create sf point geometries for the start and end points
start_point_sf <- st_sfc(st_point(c(start_node_coords[1], start_node_coords[2])), crs = st_crs(net))
end_point_sf <- st_sfc(st_point(c(end_node_coords[1], end_node_coords[2])), crs = st_crs(net))
```

```{r, mapping slope result}

mapview(edges_with_speeds, zcol = "slope_color", col.regions=list("blue", "grey","red"),col=list("blue", "grey","red"),legend = TRUE) +  # Apply the custom speed color palette
  mapview(p, col.region = "green4") +
  mapview(start_point_sf, col.region = "green", cex = 4, layer.name = "Start", legend = TRUE) +  # Start point in green, nearest feature with p we use as an example, two green points should overlap a bit
  mapview(end_point_sf, col.region = "orange", cex = 8, layer.name = "End", legend = TRUE)  # End point in orange
```

I still use that candidate path as the example. The total travel time from green to orange under tobler hiking function is:
```{r}
sum(paths_speeds_and_times_all[[1]][["travel_time"]])
```
It obviously exceeds our max threshold 15 min (900 second). So now I will slice paths based on three thresholds, 300 (5 min), 600 (10 min), and 900 (15 min).

```{r}
slice_path_by_time <- function(path, time_limit) {
  # Compute cumulative travel time along the path
  accumulated_time <- cumsum(path$travel_time)
  
  # Find the first index where accumulated time exceeds time_limit
  slice_index <- which(accumulated_time > time_limit)[1] - 1
  
  # If no time limit is exceeded, take the full path
  if (is.na(slice_index) || slice_index <= 0) {
    return(NULL)  # Return NULL to indicate no valid path
  }
  
  # Slice indices safely
  indices <- seq_len(slice_index)

  # Return the sliced path with node_paths & edge_paths included
  return(list(
    node_paths = path$node_paths[indices],
    edge_paths = path$edge_paths[indices],
    speed = path$speed[indices],
    travel_time = path$travel_time[indices],
    total_time = accumulated_time[indices]
  ))
}

# Apply function to all paths while filtering out NULL results
apply_slice_to_all_paths <- function(paths_data, time_limits) {
  result <- map(time_limits, function(time_limit) {
    sliced_paths <- map(paths_data, ~ slice_path_by_time(.x, time_limit)) %>%
      compact()  # Remove NULL results
    return(sliced_paths)
  })
  
  # Assign names for each time limit
  names(result) <- paste0("time_limit_", time_limits, "sec")
  
  return(result)
}
```

```{r, run sliced path, include=FALSE}
# Define time limits in seconds
time_limits <- c(300, 600, 900)  # 5 min, 10 min, 15 min

# Apply slicing to all paths
sliced_paths_by_time <- apply_slice_to_all_paths(paths_speeds_and_times_all, time_limits)
```

Then how it works?
`sliced_paths_by_time` is still list, with three lists named by time limit.
Each list here (e.g., sliced_paths_by_time[["time_limit_300sec"]][[1]]) stores sliced paths under a certain time limit based on `cumsum time`. So, 300-second one is the longest (20530), then 600-second one (18372), and the 900-second ha least paths (14156). 

```{r}
# 1. Function to create an isochrone polygon for the given path nodes (concave hull)
create_isochrone <- function(nodes, alpha = 0.3) {
  # Convert nodes to geometry and create a concave hull
  iso_polygon <- nodes %>%
    sf::st_geometry() %>%
    sf::st_combine() %>%
    sf::st_concave_hull(alpha) %>%
    st_as_sf()
  return(iso_polygon)
}

# 2. Create isochrones for each time limit
create_isochrones_for_all_paths <- function(sliced_paths_by_time, nodes_sf, node_df) {
  isochrones_list <- list()  # Initialize an empty list to store the isochrones
  
  for (time_limit in names(sliced_paths_by_time)) {
    sliced_paths <- sliced_paths_by_time[[time_limit]]
    
    # Step 1: Extract all node indices from all paths
    all_node_indices <- sliced_paths %>%
      map(~ .x$node_paths) %>%  # Extract node_paths from all paths
      unlist() %>%  # Flatten list
      unique()  # Keep only unique node IDs
    
    # Step 2: Retrieve corresponding coordinates from node_df
    unique_nodes_df <- node_df %>%
      filter(node_id %in% all_node_indices) %>%
      select(x, y)  # Keep only coordinates
    
    # Step 3: Convert unique nodes to an sf object
    unique_nodes_sf <- st_as_sf(unique_nodes_df, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = st_crs(nodes_sf))
    
    # Step 4: Generate the isochrone polygon from the unique nodes
    isochrone <- create_isochrone(unique_nodes_sf)
    
    # Store the isochrone in the list
    isochrones_list[[time_limit]] <- isochrone
  }
  
  return(isochrones_list)
}
```

```{r, slice time, include=FALSE}
# 3. Apply this to all the sliced paths to create isochrones for each time limit
isochrones <- create_isochrones_for_all_paths(sliced_paths_by_time, nodes_sf, nodes_df)
```

```{r}

m123 <- m3 + m2 + m1
m123
```

# Tobler hiking function with elevation factor

Similar with the last session, but I multiply speed with elevation factor.

```{r}
# 3️⃣ Fully vectorized function to compute speed & travel timeincluding elevation facto
calculate_path_speeds_and_times_elev <- function(path) {
  path_df <- calculate_slopes_distances(path) %>%
    mutate(
      slope = slope,
      mean_elev = mean_elev,
      elev_factor = elev_factor,
      speed = elev_factor * tobler_hiking_function(slope),  # Tobler function
      travel_time = distance / speed  # Travel time
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      node_paths = path[-length(path)],  # Store node paths
      edge_paths = path[-1]  # Store edge paths
    )

  return(path_df)
}
```
Run speed and time calculation with elevation factor.

